original.description: Objective: The objective of the activity is to design, build, test an integrated D-band transceiver module for high data rate satcom applications.TargetedImprovements: - Enabling D-band satellite links with higher than 10Gbit/sec- Increasing the transmission capacities by a factor of 4.- Smaller footprint and weight than Ka, V-band ISL or even optical ISL.- Less risk for interference as spectrum not completely allocated.- More resilient compared to Optical ISL (e.g. pointing misalignment or thermal effects).Description: The current state of satellite communication technologies, particularly in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) constellations, relies on existing RF and microwave frequencies, which oftenstruggle to meet the growing demand for higher bandwidth and faster data rates. Withthe advent of 5G and the transition towards 6G, current systems face significantchallenges in scaling data throughput and maintaining efficient communication, especially beyond the atmosphere. This challenge is exacerbated by the limitations of traditionalfrequency bands and the complexity of integrating both passive and active elements within semiconductor-based antenna arrays.The introduction of sub-Terahertz frequencies, specifically in the D-Band range of 110 to 170 GHz, can offer a solution to these issues. These higher frequency bands providesignificantly larger bandwidths, allowing for faster data rates, lower power consumption, and smaller,more efficient hardware. However, fully utilizing the D-band spectrumrequires innovative concept to integrate both active components, such as amplifiers and receivers, and passive components, such as filters, with advanced semiconductor-basedantenna arrays.This project will address these challenges by developing two D-Band transceiver module engineering models, using the latest advancements in MMIC (Monolithic MicrowaveIntegrated Circuit) chipset technologies and packaging techniques, enabling future 6G NTN (Non-Terrestrial Network) phased-array applications. It will focus on the integrationof both active (e.g. amplifiers, receivers) and passiveelements (e.g. filters) with semiconductor-based antenna arrays. This integration is crucial for power efficiency, reducingpower losses, and ensuring scalable solutions that can be applied across satellite constellations. In addition to addressing integration challenges, the proposed activity willexplore advanced multiplexing techniques, such as Orbital Angular Momentum (OAM), which can significantly increase communication capacity without requiring additionalfrequency bandwidth. This novel approach promises to optimize system performance and unlock greater scalability for satellite communication systems in the 6G era. Theproject will first focus onbreadboarding critical components like the high-power amplifier, receiver, filtering functions and antenna. Subsequently, two engineering modeltransceiver modules with critical functions will be manufactured and tested. A point-to-point link demonstrator will becreated for testing, ensuring that the system meets at leastone specific 6G use case such as Joint Communication and Sensing (JCAS), Multi-orbit Inter-satellite Link (ISL), or Extreme Capacity Backhaul (xHaul).

original.description: Objective: To design a solar array concept allowing for in-orbit reconfiguration of strings length and section size and to optimisethe solar array power output for EOL best possible performance.Description: Solar cell voltage and current are a function of operating temperature and degradation level. String lengths and section sizes are optimised for EOL best performance. However, this means that for most of the time the solar array is not exploiting its full performance capability. If string lengths and section sizes were reconfigurable, the power output at each time of the mission could be maximised. This concept could provide various benefits, such as flexible adaptation in case of unforeseen events (e.g. solar flares, micrometeorite impacts, etc.), mission extension in GEO and potential use of cells with less performance in GEO radiation environment. These benefits can be of interest for Telecom applications, where very large solar arrays are typically required to compensate for the degradation over the entire mission. This activity targets innovative photovoltaic assembly concepts that allows for reconfiguring string lengths and section size to optimise performance in dependence of operating conditions during the mission (e.g. temperature, irradiation level). This activity encompasses the following tasks: - Definition of a solar array / photovoltaic assembly concept allowing for reconfiguration of string lengths and section sizes. - Prototyping of interconnection concepts. - Initial proof of concept demonstration.

Launch and spacecraft re-entry effects onthe atmosphere are known gaps to fulfil these requirements. This results in significant uncertainty andsystematic exclusion of such effects when developing materials on the basis of sustainable performance.Previous and ongoing Discovery activities, Insights into the Chemistry of Atmospheric Re-entry of JunkedSpacecraft (ICARUS) and Impacts of space Debris ablation on Earth's Atmospheric System (IDEAS), havehighlighted the potential importance of ablation products in the atmosphere while established initial modellingapproaches and experimental validation capabilities.The proposed activity addresses this critical knowledge gap by developing a consolidated experimental andmodelling framework to characterise emissionsfrom spacecraft re-entry and integrate these into atmosphericand design assessment tools. This will enable the incorporation of atmospheric impacts into Life CycleAssessment (LCA) and support both Ecodesign and Design-for-Demise (D4D) decision making. original.description: Objective: To develop an Electro-Dynamic-Shield system to mitigate systems degradation for missions to the Moon, Mars and planetarybodies including a significant dusty environment.Description: Exploration systems in contact with planetary surfaces covered in regolith such as the Moon and Mars are subject to local dust displacement and accumulation on critical surfaces affecting system performance as for instance thermal balance, power generation efficiency and optical transmission and system lifetime. A number of mitigation strategies have been put forward and tested mostly on ground with a very limited demonstration in space. The Electro-Dynamic Shield (EDS) technology is a method used to mitigate the accumulation of dust on surfaces, particularly in space environments. This technology employs electric fields to repel dust particles, preventing them from settling on critical surfaces such as solar panels, sensors, and other equipment. This technology has been studied for more than twenty years outside of Europe for the mitigation of dust deposition on terrestrial and space system and it has been recently demonstrated on the Moon. In Europe, most of the studies performed so far have been on laboratory scale. Among others, an experimental EDS was successfully implemented on a number of samples including optical glass and Kapton sheets and demonstrated very high dust removal efficiency in a vacuum environment including UV, showing good potential for targeted system feasibility studies. Based on this success, the feasibility of implementing such technology on actual space hardware by breadboarding and testing critical functionalities can be addressed. This activity encompasses the following tasks: - Define the requirements for the implementation of an EDS system into relevant spacecraft structures and materials of interest with a priority towards solar arrays (with possible applicability to optical surface and other materials) and define the requirements from the target system towards EDS. - Assess the required modifications of standard designs to accommodate an EDS system, establish a list of technological gaps, define specific tests and a test plan to address the technological gaps. - Design and manufacture relevant breadboards to demonstrate EDS operational efficiency on targeted system. - Perform test for critical functionalities,including in representative laboratory environments (dusty vacuum and in presence of UV). - Based on the tests outcomes and future missions needs provide a technical roadmap with a cost outline.
